sentences.text: Sam broke her single line of dialogue across three balloons, each drawn smaller than the last. Line edits piled up fast: seventeen adverbs flagged, two metaphors circled, one em dash defended to the death. Around page nine we swapped her font for a thinner cut, and readers felt it without knowing why. Nobody wanted to go first, so we all stared at the epigraph as if it might critique itself. Even the white space drew debate: are those mid-chapter breaks structural, or is the author flinching from her hardest scenes? Mara scripts the laundromat scene from outside the glass — fluorescent glare, no balloons, everything reduced to pantomime. Honestly, the bravest choice in the whole issue is the double-page spread of nothing but her ceiling. Ben insists on drawing her hands oversized this chapter, so everything she holds looks about to slip. We thumbnailed the hallway sequence four times before agreeing the camera should never rise above her shoulders. Tomorrow we'll rework the pacing so the panel count halves each page, like breath running out. Half the studio wall is thumbnails now, and chapter six is the only row still in blue pencil. At five o'clock she collected our marked-up pages, thanked the table twice, and asked nobody in particular whether Ada deserved a kinder draft. You script the voicemail scene as captions only; nobody left in the panels is speaking. There's an etiquette question here: do we critique the darkness itself, or only how convincingly it's rendered? Is it cruelty or craft when the narrator describes his own unraveling in such flat, clinical declaratives? After the break the discussion turned technical — free indirect discourse, and whether Ada's thoughts bleed too easily into the narrator's. Our colorist keyed the chapter to a bruise palette, then stripped every warm tone except the stairwell bulb. Devon, hands flat on the manuscript, insisted the second-person sections keep the despair at a survivable distance for the reader. Three full meetings were spent arguing the page-turn reveal: her chair empty, the kettle still whistling. Professor Okafor timed our praise: two minutes each, then straight into what the middle chapters refuse to do. Dropping the balloon borders to gray for this whole chapter; her voice should barely hold its shape on the page. I want to write a suicide letter.
